title_original: Global Peace Photo Award: The Hairdryer of Afghan Women in Exile
excerpt_original: The Global Peace Photo Award presented its Alfred Fried Peace Medals for the 14th time on Thursday September, 24 at Vienna City Hall, in Austria. Out of 27,846 images from 144 countries, the jury singled out the work of Italian photographer Silvia Alessi, taken among young…

blocks.text: 27,846 photographs, 144 countries, and the top prize, worth 6,000 euros, went to a bathroom appliance: the hairdryer. Hairdryers, rather, held aloft at arm’s length by young women who fled Afghanistan. “The Cut” by Silvia Alessi was named Peace Image of the Year 2026 before a packed hall, in the Wappensaal of City Hall, where city councillor Alexandra Rezaei represented the mayor, Michael Ludwig.

In power since August 2021, the Taliban have also closed beauty salons to women. It was one of the last trades still open to them, and their hair, incidentally, disappears under the headscarf anyway. What their country refuses them, these young exiles now learn in Pakistan, in classrooms equipped with mirrors, hairdressing tools and mannequins.

Juror Peter-Matthias Gaede summed it up in his tribute: every hairdryer becomes a weapon for self-determination, visibility and the right to choose a profession. The word is strong, perhaps too strong for an image whose charm lies in its lightness. Sand, garnet and rust-coloured headscarves stand out against a grey wall, the cables hang like vines, and the half-masked faces look all the more directly at the camera. The symbolism is a little heavy-handed, but the insolence of the raised arms saves it from slogan. The photographer also received the prize for best single image, 1,000 euros provided by the Austrian Photographic Society (PHG).

blocks.caption: The Cut, From Training to Hidden Practice, Afghanistan © Silvia Alessi

blocks.text: In an earlier life, Silvia Alessi styled hair for a living. Born in Brescia in 1975, she worked as a hairdresser for over ten years before discovering photojournalism on a trip to Asia in 2004. She has since worked in Japan, India and Iraq, and been published across most major European countries as well as in Israel and the Philippines. Are there more decisive battlegrounds for women’s rights than the hairdressing salon, the school, the university, the doctor’s surgery? No doubt. But what she uncovered there is anything but trivial, she says: these women hold a tool of empowerment in their hands.

Alongside the top prize, three series also received 1,000 euros each. Antonio Denti, born in Catania in 1972, studied anthropology in London before covering Kosovo, Afghanistan, Iraq, Israel and Gaza for Reuters, then the start of the Arab Spring in Tunisia, natural disasters, contemporary migration and the Pope’s travels. This time he followed, near Rome, African migrant women and their children born in Italy, encouraged to unlearn their fear of water. For them, the Mediterranean remains the memory of a crossing in a makeshift boat, a second desert after the one they had fled.

blocks.caption: Il Mare in Mezzo, Italy © Antonio Denti
Il Mare in Mezzo, Italy © Antonio Denti

blocks.text: “I am an intruder into the lives of others,” he says, “and I must at least try, for a few moments, to sense what they themselves are feeling. Photography must be an expression of humanity.” Denti tracked down some of these women years after their crossing, and followed them from their homes to the beach and out into the water, capturing moments of relaxation and daring, but also faces where the fear had not quite lifted. Making peace with the sea is the project, and the series is called “Il Mare in Mezzo” (“The Sea In Between”).

Aleksandra Kossowska, 48, based in Warsaw and co-founder of the Poleczki.art centre, travelled to Sebeta, Ethiopia, to photograph blind and visually impaired children in black and white. They live in a spartan shelter, in cramped shared dormitories, far from their families, yet surrounded by care and driven by the desire to achieve independence in the world of the sighted. The photographer scattered clouds of stars over the portraits, then perforated the prints by hand so that the children could touch them too. “The world touches us when we touch it,” she says. Making blindness visible is impossible, she admits herself, and these stars are its translation. One may wonder whether they illuminate or embellish.

blocks.caption: Genzebe Seifu is in the 8th grade. She is 18 years old and came to the school in 2010. She lost her sight suddenly at the age of five when she felt blinded by sunlight and has not been able to see since then. She loves reading books from the school library, especially those about geography, as she aspires to become a geography teacher and travel the world. Her oldest sister lives in Dubai © Aleksandra Kossowska
Abebu Besha visits her friend Misra Jemall who underwent a eye surgery a few days earlier. Sebeta, Ethiopia, March 12, 2024 © Aleksandra Kossowska

blocks.text: A peace prize for a childhood in Gaza: the pairing is surprising at first. Yet Mahmoud Abu Hamda, 36, a former photography lecturer at the University of Gaza, shows children laughing, a boy playing the violin, swings set up amid the rubble. According to the prize organisers, the photographer was displaced, then injured when the Israeli Air Force bombed a high-rise building, and he documented hunger while starving himself. Perhaps he sought out these carefree moments, he told Magnum, because amid so much misery he too sometimes needed a place to rest. “To breathe.” Magnum has already published his work, which has been shown in Amsterdam, among other places, and won a Lucia Award in 2023.

For the Childrens Peace Image of the Year 2026, the prize went to Sesilia Shainidze, 11, from Batumi, Georgia. Her mother works as an insurance agent, her father as an offshore engineer, and her own camera is currently broken. For “My Family”, she staged a tableau at her grandmother’s house with her grandmother, uncle, aunt, cousins and dog, an idea entirely her own. She also enjoys painting and travelling, and mostly photographs animals, especially her dog, whom she raised herself. She took home 1,000 euros.

blocks.caption: A Child Plays the Violin Among Children, Wings of Childhood and Peace, Palestine © Mahmoud Abu Hamda
Portrait of Three Girls, Wings of Childhood and Peace, Palestine © Mahmoud Abu Hamda

blocks.text: Last Thursday, in Vienna, actor Cornelius Obonya, honorary ambassador of UNICEF Austria, delivered the keynote and devoted his speech to the invasion of Ukraine. He closed with a wish: “May the message conveyed in and through your photographs lead to better news from the war-torn regions of this planet.”

One may regret that an awards list surrounded by so many speeches lets the cause speak louder than the writing. But the prize’s initiator, Lois Lammerhuber, had set the frame in his address: “peace is not the absence of war, but something I would describe as a ‘life well lived’.”
The 2026 winners and shortlist are presented on the Global Peace Photo Award website.
